name: Margaret Mead
kicker: American cultural anthropologist · Studied growing up across cultures
briefing: At just twenty-three years old, Margaret Mead sailed to the South Pacific island of Samoa to live among teenage girls and study their lives firsthand. Her 1928 book, _Coming of Age in Samoa_, argued that culture, not biology, shapes how difficult or easy growing up can be, and it made her one of the most famous scientists in America. She spent decades doing fieldwork across the Pacific, sometimes alongside her husband and fellow anthropologist Gregory Bateson.

tossups.p: With her husband Gregory Bateson, this woman published a photographic study called _Balinese Character_. In an earlier book, she had compared three New Guinea peoples: the peaceful Arapesh [“AH-ruh-pesh”], the aggressive Mundugumor, and the Tchambuli [“CHAHM-boo-lee”], among whom women were the practical, dominant ones.
tossups.r: That book, _Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies_, argued that gender roles come from culture rather than biology. This thinker’s most famous research, on the island of Samoa, was later challenged by the critic Derek Freeman. For 10 points, name this American anthropologist who wrote _Coming of Age in Samoa_.

tossups.p: Born in Philadelphia in 1901, this woman earned her doctorate in anthropology from Columbia University, where she studied under Franz Boas and alongside fellow anthropologist Ruth Benedict. She later helped revise the Episcopal Church’s 1979 Book of Common Prayer.

trap.title: Teacher, husband, or critic?
trap.body: Real tossups name several other people in the same breath as Mead: her teachers Franz Boas and Ruth Benedict, her husband and research partner Gregory Bateson, her conversation partner James Baldwin, and her later critic Derek Freeman, who challenged her Samoa research after she died. All five are real people, but none of them is the answer.
trap.fix: Listen for the relationship word: “her teacher,” “her husband,” or “this critic” signals that a different name is about to follow, but the tossup is still asking about the anthropologist who actually did the fieldwork, not the other person.
